title: Scheduler throttle and short-request tail latency postmortem
body:
Summary:

On 2025-12-01 we observed persistent tail-latency SLO misses for a subset of hosted small-batch text-generation requests (~1-4 tokens per request). Impact window: ~2025-12-01T02:20Z -> 2025-12-01T05:50Z. Customers reported elevated p99s and intermittent timeouts. This postmortem documents the investigation, root cause, fixes deployed, and follow-ups.

Primary impact:
- p99 generation latency for short requests increased from ~120ms to ~600-1200ms on affected nodes.
- Error rates (upstream 504s) rose from ~0.02% to 0.6% for a small set of customers using default small-batch policy.
- Affected capacity: ~8% of serving fleet in us-west region during the window (heterogeneous GPU types).

What happened (short):
- Change in GPU-side scheduling heuristics (recent scheduler change merged two weeks prior) introduced a throttle condition that deprioritized tiny-inference work during microbursts of large continuous-batched workloads. Under typical steady-state mixed workloads this improved throughput, but under our production arrival patterns it caused starvation for tiny requests and inflated dispatch queues and software-side queuing. The throttling decision interacted badly with our host-side worker backpressure counters and KV cache prefetch heuristics, producing long tail latency for short requests.

Timeline (key events):
- 2025-11-18: Scheduler optimization merged (PR 2211) — designed to reduce small kernel launch overhead by grouping similar long-running batches and yielding GPUs less frequently.
- 2025-12-01 02:18Z: Alerting triggered for p99 anomaly on hosted-api-prod-us-west cluster.
- 2025-12-01 02:22Z: On-call (Ethan) began initial triage; scaled up node pool to soak traffic.
- 2025-12-01 02:35Z: Captured flamegraphs and RT histograms from affected boxes. Noted long software queue time before kernel launch for small requests.
- 2025-12-01 03:05Z: Reproduced locally with replay harness by replaying production traces with injected heavy continuous-batch traffic.
- 2025-12-01 03:50Z: Identified throttling counter being set inside GPU scheduler code path; confirmed correlation w/ PR 2211.
- 2025-12-01 04:20Z: Hotfix PR 2345 created to disable the aggressive throttle for tiny requests and to add a per-request SLO priority bypass.
- 2025-12-01 04:45Z: Hotfix deployed to canary nodes. Observed immediate reduction in p99.
- 2025-12-01 05:15Z: Rollout to remaining nodes in us-west completed. Metrics returned to baseline by ~05:50Z.

Investigation details and evidence:
- Profiling artifacts:
  - Flamegraphs (software-side) showed growing "dispatch_queue.wait" spans for short requests, dominating the p99 stack.
  - nvprof and NVML logs from affected GPUs showed low kernel occupancy for tiny-kernel launches interleaved with long-running batched kernels — scheduler batching grouped large kernels and held GPU resources, deferring small kernels.
  - Host-side traces indicated that requests were accepted and queued at the frontend, but worker threads reported long waits on "schedule_acceptor.lock" leading to delayed kernel submissions.

- Key logs/metrics examined:
  - per-node qlen and time-in-queue histograms (prometheus): qlen tail spiked concurrently with p99.
  - scheduler.throttle_counter logs matched spikes in qlen latency.
  - KV-cache prefetch logic started pre-warming large prefixes in the same time window, increasing memory pressure and affecting worker scheduling priorities.

Reproduction notes (how we reproduced locally):
- Used the production trace replay harness (tools/replay/trace_replay.py) with: --trace us-west-20251201-small-requests.json --background-workload large-seq-512-continuous.json --gpu-type a40 --nodes 8.
- Observed p99 increases locally within 20 minutes.
- Toggle the throttle flag (runtime flag gpu.scheduler.enable_aggr_throttle=false) reverted behavior in replay.

Root cause analysis:
- Immediate cause: aggressive GPU-side aggregation/throttle heuristic introduced in PR 2211 that grouped long batched kernels and deferred tiny kernel submissions until an aggregation window completed. That heuristic assumed homogenous workload and did not account for high-priority tiny requests.
- Contributing factors:
  1) Lack of per-request SLO-aware priority in scheduler decisions.
  2) Host worker backpressure counters were insufficiently granular: they only measured queue length, not request criticality (latency-sensitive vs throughput-oriented).
  3) KV cache prefetch patterns increased CPU-side scheduler load, amplifying scheduling latencies.
  4) Rollout lacked a specific e2e mixed-workload replay in the mergegate checklist for PR 2211.

Why the hotfix worked:
- Hotfix disabled the aggregation throttle for tiny requests and added a bypass where requests marked latency_slo=true are tagged on accept and ignored by the aggregation window. This let small kernels be submitted with priority, eliminating the software queue starvation.

Mitigation and remediation taken:
- Immediate: rolled back aggregation throttle on affected nodes and rolled out hotfix PR 2345 across us-west.
- Short-term (next 2 weeks):
  - Add a runtime-config default to keep gpu.scheduler.enable_aggr_throttle=false for hosted-api clusters until we have better heuristics.
  - Add a temporary metric gpu.scheduler.latency_starvation_count and alert if > 5/min.
  - Update canary criteria: require mixed-workload trace replay (tiny + continuous large) pass before merge for scheduler changes.
- Long-term (Q1 2026):
  - Implement SLO-priority token in scheduler so latency-sensitive requests can preempt aggregation windows.
  - Extend host worker queue to be multi-class (latency vs throughput) and add fastpath for tiny requests (lock-free handoff).
  - Rework KV cache prefetch heuristic to avoid synchronized prefetch across workers.

Validation and metrics after hotfix (observed):
- p99 returned to baseline within ~45 minutes of full rollout; p50 unchanged.
- Error rate reduced to baseline; no further 504 spikes reported.
- Canary replay runs (100k small requests + background big batches) showed p99 within 5% of baseline.

Customer communications:
- Sent initial incident acknowledgement to impacted customers within 90 minutes of alert.
- Follow-up update after hotfix deployment with summary and mitigation steps.
- Dedicated post-incident outreach plan: schedule 30-min technical call with top impacted customers to explain the fix and to collect any residual telemetry.

Postmortem action items (owner, ETA):
- Scheduler SLO-priority design doc (Asha) — ETA 2026-01-12.
- Implement runtime flag gating and add replay test to mergegate (Ethan) — ETA 2025-12-10.
- Add gpu.scheduler.latency_starvation_count and alert (Kai) — ETA 2025-12-08.
- KV prefetch de-sync prototype (Lucia) — ETA 2026-01-30.
- Customer outreach and RC notes (Asha + CS lead) — ETA 2025-12-06.

Notes to engineering readers / debugging tips:
- If you see rising p99 but steady p50, check scheduler.throttle_counter and per-node nvml kernel timing logs.
- Use the small-request replay trace combined with continuous large-batch trace for local repro.
- Flamegraphs are particularly useful to distinguish "software queue wait" from GPU kernel time.

Appendix: useful commands and traces used during investigation:
- Trace replay: python tools/replay/trace_replay.py --trace traces/us-west-20251201_small.json --background traces/continuous-large-512.json --gpu a40 --nodes 8
- Extract NVML window: tools/nvml/window_extract.sh --start 2025-12-01T02:10Z --end 2025-12-01T06:00Z --node node-17
- Quick flamegraph: python tools/prof/flamegen.py --ingest=/tmp/prof-collect --filter=dispatch_queue

Links:
- PR that introduced heuristic: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/2211
- Hotfix PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/2345
- Reproduction trace (internal): gs://redwood-traces/us-west/2025-12-01-small-requests.json

Owner signoff:
Asha Patel (eng-serving-runtime) — 2025-12-04

End of document.
